query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a ductile refractory metal such as niobium (Nb) to a base HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase HfZrTi-based HEA that, while having high strength, displays limited ductility and toughness at ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base HfZrTi composition with a controlled amount of Nb (e.g., forming an alloy analogous to Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi but focused on the Nb addition) during processing.
generation.conditions: Standard solidification or powder metallurgy processing routes at ambient temperature, followed by room-temperature mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a more ductile body-centered cubic (BCC) phase with coherent interfaces that reduce stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Niobium’s relatively low melting point and ductile character promote enhanced dislocation mobility and activate multiple slip systems. Its addition helps to relieve lattice distortion and encourages the formation of phases or microstructural features with coherent boundaries that slow crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA will display increased tensile elongation and fracture toughness relative to the original HfZrTi alloy, with improved plastic deformation behavior and less brittle failure.
generation.baseline: The unmodified HfZrTi HEA, which has high strength but a tendency towards brittleness and low fracture toughness under standard processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The positive effect on ductility and toughness is expected within an optimal Nb concentration range; too little may be ineffective while too much could lead to phase instability or excessive softening.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements and the ideal Nb content remain to be determined experimentally. The effect might also be influenced by processing conditions and the potential presence of other minor elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of alloys: one of the base HfZrTi HEA and one with incremental Nb additions (e.g., 5, 10, and 15 atomic percent substitution). Process the alloys under identical conditions and subject them to standardized tensile and fracture toughness tests.
measurements: Microstructural characterization by TEM and XRD to assess phase formation and interface coherency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in ductility and fracture toughness compared to the base HfZrTi alloy, or if they exhibit adverse phase transformations or degradation, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

[ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. We observed that the relaxation peaks in the current HEAs are asymmetrically broadened (see Fig. 1, A to C ). This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions ( [28] ). Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions, it is difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes. However, two main configurations of the interstitial atoms can indeed be distinguished in the current material, namely, position switches of interstitials in ordered interstitial complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed interstitial atoms ( [22] ). These two kinds of configurations both contribute to the current Snoek relaxation and can cause at least some of the asymmetries observed. Therefore, we conduct a decomposition of the relaxation structure in terms of the two main classes of interstitial configurations (see the Supplementary Materials).
